summary: Leviticus 14 begins after a person’s skin plague has healed: the priest goes outside the camp, performs a bird rite, and oversees washing, shaving, waiting, and offerings that restore clean status. A reduced offering keeps the process open to someone who is poor. The second half gives future procedures for a spreading plague in a Canaanite house, ranging from inspection and repair to demolition or cleansing.
whyItMatters: Where chapter 13 emphasizes exclusion, this chapter builds a concrete route back into camp and sacred life after healing. Its rites cleanse ritual status rather than provide medical treatment, and its poverty provision prevents the full sacrifice cost from making restoration unreachable.

context.author: The text presents these instructions as Yahweh’s words through Moses and Aaron; authorship and final composition are debated
context.audience: The children of Israel and the priests who examine and cleanse people, garments, and houses
context.date: The personal rites are framed in Israel’s camp, while the house law anticipates Canaan; final composition is debated
context.setting: Outside and inside Israel’s camp, at the Tent of Meeting, and prospectively in houses in Canaan
context.literaryForm: Priestly cleansing rites and case law

outline.heading: Examination and the bird rite outside camp
outline.note: After finding the plague healed, the priest performs the rite and the person washes, shaves, enters camp, and waits outside a tent.

outline.heading: Offerings for restored sanctuary access
outline.note: On the eighth day the priest applies sacrificial blood and oil, then offers the required sacrifices.

outline.heading: A reduced offering for the poor
outline.note: One lamb, less flour, and affordable birds replace the larger set without changing the cleansing outcome.

outline.heading: Inspection and repair of a house
outline.note: In Canaan, a reported wall plague leads to emptying, inspection, seven-day closure, and removal of affected stones and mortar if it spreads.

outline.heading: Recurring house plague or successful cleansing
outline.note: A recurring destructive mildew brings demolition; a healed house receives a bird rite and is pronounced clean.

outline.heading: The law’s full scope
outline.note: The conclusion gathers skin, itch, garment, house, swelling, scab, and spot under instruction about clean and unclean.

keyVerses.text: and the priest shall go out of the camp. The priest shall examine him. Behold, if the plague of leprosy is healed in the leper,
keyVerses.why: Restoration begins with the priest going to the excluded person and confirming that healing has already occurred.

keyVerses.text: He shall sprinkle on him who is to be cleansed from the leprosy seven times, and shall pronounce him clean, and shall let the living bird go into the open field.
keyVerses.why: The rite ends in a clean declaration and release, beginning the person’s staged return.

keyVerses.text: “If he is poor, and can’t afford so much, then he shall take one male lamb for a trespass offering to be waved, to make atonement for him, and one tenth of an ephah of fine flour mixed with oil for a meal offering, and a log of oil;
keyVerses.why: The law reduces the number of lambs and amount of flour for a poor person while retaining oil and a required lamb.

keyVerses.text: The priest shall command that they empty the house, before the priest goes in to examine the plague, that all that is in the house not be made unclean. Afterward the priest shall go in to inspect the house.
keyVerses.why: The house procedure deliberately protects its contents from being swept into an unclean ruling before inspection.

questions.question: Does the priest’s ritual heal the skin condition?
questions.answer: No. Verse 3 begins the process only after the priest finds that the plague is healed. The following rites wash, cleanse, and pronounce the person clean so that return to camp and sanctuary life can proceed.

questions.question: Why does the priest go outside the camp?
questions.answer: The person has been living outside under the earlier unclean ruling, so examination begins where that person is. After the first rite and washing, the person may enter the camp but still waits seven days outside the tent before the next stage.

questions.question: What do the two birds, cedar, scarlet, and hyssop symbolize?
questions.answer: One bird is killed over running water; the living bird, cedar, scarlet, and hyssop are dipped and used for sprinkling, and the living bird is released. The sequence marks cleansing and release, but the chapter does not assign a separate symbolic meaning to each material.

questions.question: Why are blood and oil placed on the right ear, thumb, and big toe?
questions.answer: Verses 14-18 prescribe those three points first for blood and then for oil, followed by oil on the head. The chapter presents the sequence as part of cleansing and atonement but does not provide a separate explanation for each body part.

questions.question: What does “atonement” mean in this cleansing process?
questions.answer: Here it names priestly action in the healed person’s cleansing rite and concludes with “he shall be clean.” The condition itself is not charged as a moral offense, so atonement in this case must not be reduced to punishment for personal wrongdoing.

questions.question: How is the cleansing rite changed for a poor person?
questions.answer: The poor person brings one male lamb rather than three lambs, a smaller amount of flour, oil, and two birds that he can afford. The blood-and-oil application and the priest’s atoning work remain, and the text gives the same clean result.

questions.question: Why does Yahweh say, “I put a spreading mildew in a house”?
questions.answer: The law attributes the future house plague to Yahweh as it anticipates Israel’s life in Canaan, but it does not identify a homeowner’s sin or tell readers to diagnose misfortune as punishment. The instructed response is observation, containment, repair, and a ruling based on whether the mark spreads or heals.

questions.question: Why must the house be emptied before the priest inspects it?
questions.answer: Verse 36 gives the reason: emptying the house before inspection prevents its contents from being swept into an unclean ruling. The instruction protects movable belongings while the priest determines the house’s ritual status.

questions.question: When is a house repaired, destroyed, or declared clean?
questions.answer: Spreading marks after the first closure lead to removal of stones, scraping, and replastering. If the plague returns and spreads, the house is dismantled; if it does not spread after repair, the priest declares it healed and performs the stated cleansing rite.

reviewer: Codex editorial agents; independent chapter review

before.text: The previous chapter requires a person ruled unclean to live outside the camp and gives inspection and disposal rules for affected garments.

here.text: After healing is confirmed, a priest begins the person’s staged return with a bird rite, washing, waiting, and offerings, including a lower-cost provision. A second law anticipates inspection, repair, or removal of affected houses in Canaan.

after.text: The following chapter treats bodily discharges, semen, and menstrual blood as sources of ritual uncleanness with specified washing, waiting, and in some cases offerings.
